# Ledger — complete build record and light-mode reconstruction manual

This is a standalone guide for building your own personal budgeting app. Manual accounts, transactions, budgets, reports, subscription tracking and forecasts work locally without Plaid, Codex or a paid AI service. Optional bank syncing and automated merchant agents require your own setup; their providers may have separate fees or eligibility requirements.

## 1. How to use this guide

The reference appearance is **warm newsprint light mode**: cream paper, Lora headings, inky hairlines, quiet navigation and restrained warm color. The narrative explains design, accounting rules, architecture, deployment and verification. The appendix supplies all 75 source files, including tests, local fonts, licenses and the Windows icon. Four binary assets are embedded as Base64.

**Reconstruction contract for GPT 5.6 Luna:** Restore the source into a NEW empty directory, verify every checksum, run isolated tests, and open a synthetic light-mode instance before changing anything. Preserve the vanilla JavaScript/Python implementation, local typography, CSS order and accounting semantics. If reimplementing deliberately, treat the embedded source and tests as the behavioral reference. Read relevant modules in chunks instead of loading the entire appendix into context at once.

The narrative describes the current snapshot. Some embedded source documentation records earlier milestones, such as a lower test count or integrations not yet tested. Executable source is authoritative for implementation details. This shareable edition changes packaging instructions and the Windows builder's source digest; application behavior and the light-mode design remain intact.

Personal names, email addresses, account handles, private server identities, network addresses, local user paths, private download links, message IDs and account-specific history have been removed. No real financial records, login verifiers, credentials, browser sessions or Codex authentication files are included. Synthetic test data and required third-party license credits remain.

Reading order: sections 1–5 for scope, section 6 for visuals, section 7 for backend rules, then platform and validation sections. Use `RESTORE-LEDGER-SOURCE.py` to recover the appendix or extract `Ledger-Source.zip`. Neither method requires access to a particular GitHub account. Never test against a real financial data directory.

## 2. Product goals and independent installations

The app is named **Ledger**, with the sidebar wordmark **ledger.** It is a personal finance dashboard with a deliberately calm interface over a more capable underlying system. Useful next actions, spending totals and recurring commitments should be clear without visiting many tabs.

Every person runs an **independent single-owner installation** with their own financial records, owner password, bank credentials and optional worker authentication. The code supports a private Ubuntu server and a Windows desktop wrapper. Sharing the source or installer does not share a database, account, server or AI subscription. Shared household synchronization and multi-owner access are not implemented.

### Product priorities

- Keep ordinary local manual tracking usable without paid services.
- Keep dashboard navigation simple and advanced setup optional.
- Avoid double-counting recurring commitments and itemized purchases.
- Preserve explicit user choices when importing or reclassifying transactions.
- Keep data separate from program files and preserve it during updates.
- Provide a desktop icon for Windows users, with no terminal commands required for routine use.
- Require each person to configure their own optional bank and agent integrations.
- Review delegated implementation work against the source, tests and final appearance.

The Windows package targets Intel/AMD x64 Windows 10 or 11 and includes its Python runtime. For source-based manual use, Python 3.11+ and a browser are sufficient. No AI is needed to run the core dashboard.

## 3. Implemented features and validation limits

| Area | Implemented | Boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Dashboard and themes | Warm light mode, separate charcoal dark mode, configurable cards/fonts/colors | This manual's visual reconstruction target is light mode |
| Accounts and transactions | Manual entry/edit/delete, balances, transfers, personal/business scope | No multi-currency conversion or certified bookkeeping |
| Reports | Twelve month columns, yearly and all-time recorded spend, category/month matrix | All-time totals only cover recorded history |
| Subscriptions | Recurring detection, uncertain-candidate review, price-change review, monthly reconciliation | A recurring purchase is not automatically a subscription |
| Cancellation | Guarded queue, local worker, evidence and user-handoff states | Provider sign-in may be needed; no universal cancellation guarantee |
| Purchase details | Receipt lookup, verified allocations, review and undo | Real receipts may be unavailable or ambiguous |
| Forecasts | Cash, investment, debt and inflation scenarios | Projections are assumptions, not guaranteed balances |
| Bank connections | Plaid integration, saved-key indicators, OAuth origin checks and clear errors | Each installation needs its own valid configuration and bank consent |
| Windows package | Bundled runtime, installer, shortcuts, preserved data | No signed MSI or automatic background updater; native Windows UI needs platform testing |
| Validation | Earlier application suite passed 115 tests; isolated startup and reconstruction were checked | Mocked integration tests are not live bank or merchant validation |

A saved checkmark reports that a credential is stored, not that the provider has validated it. Installing Ledger or saving keys alone never means a bank is connected.

## 4. Design and feature evolution

The final source resolves several design iterations; do not average rejected earlier styles into the clone.

1. Expand the foundation with themes, subscription review/cancellation, future projections and sensitive recurring-payment discovery.
2. Support private cross-device server hosting alongside independent local desktop installations.
3. Replace a bland monochrome treatment with restrained color.
4. Choose bundled **Lora** for warm serif headings; preserve its actual metrics.
5. Refine newspaper-inspired cream/off-white surfaces into a classic, modern and clean layout, avoiding novelty retro styling.
6. Warm greenish paper backgrounds and move purple accents toward copper/orange.
7. Use brighter translucent summary cards and a warm recurring-payment prompt.
8. Balance the three main cards with distinct, complementary text/background/accent rules.
9. Give dark mode a separate deep-charcoal treatment and soften overly bright green/blue text. These dark-mode choices do not redefine the light reference.
10. Inherit business/personal defaults from accounts while preserving explicit transaction overrides.
11. Use very thin blue-black ink rules, a slightly stronger sidebar divider, and one clean header rule.
12. Keep the friendly greeting comma and “Here's where things stand” subheader.
13. Show twelve months side by side, yearly and all-time recorded spending, and the All categories total row above the category/month matrix.
14. Enlarge and square the L mark, shift its glyph right for optical centering, shorten the wordmark, add its period and increase letter spacing.
15. Add receipt-backed Amazon/Apple/Google item classification: personal-care purchases, groceries and tools can reach distinct budgets without duplicating the charge.
16. Use a wider 248px collapsible desktop sidebar, a 78px collapsed rail and a separate mobile drawer.
17. Provide source-based Ubuntu setup and optional Homepage dashboard integration.
18. Package the same app with an embedded Windows Python runtime, hidden supervisor, per-user installer and desktop/Start menu shortcuts.
19. Support initial password setup from an authorized remote computer through an SSH loopback forward, preserving localhost-only first setup.
20. Separate project-description URLs from bank OAuth return URLs.
21. Add native saved-key placeholders/checkmarks, fresh-config linking, same-origin OAuth guidance and actionable provider errors.
22. Audit the implementation and simplify the credential indicators into the actual settings renderer rather than observer/wrapper machinery.
23. Build updates that replace application files while preserving existing records and authentication.

## 6. Exact warm-newsprint light-mode design and frontend behavior

### Scope and source boundary

This document reconstructs the rendered light interface from the Ledger source snapshot in this shareable edition. It is intended as a handoff for an implementation agent who needs to reproduce the visual language and behavior without depending on conversation history. The evidence comes from the source files in `web/`, `backend/db.py`, and the API assumptions visible in the JavaScript. No database, configuration file, browser profile, credential, or running application is part of this description.

The source is a vanilla JavaScript single page application. The server renders the static shell from `web/index.html`; JavaScript registers page render functions and replaces `#view` with HTML strings returned from API calls. The visual system is split across several CSS layers rather than one clean stylesheet, and the load order is part of the design. Preserve the load order before changing any selectors.

The relevant source files are:

- `web/index.html`: document attributes, early theme/sidebar state, persistent shell, navigation, script and stylesheet order.
- `web/styles.css`: original generic design system and broad component rules.
- `web/comfort.css`: the “quiet layer,” the final structural layout and most of the modern interface geometry.
- `web/paper.css`: warm newsprint palette and paper-specific overrides for light mode.
- `web/dark.css`: dark-theme replacements; its selectors are inactive when the root is light.
- `web/sidebar.css`: final desktop width, collapse rail, labels, tooltips and responsive sidebar corrections.
- `web/reports.css`: report-specific layout and mobile behavior.
- `web/fonts/fonts.css`: locally served Lora, Manrope and Nunito Sans faces.
- `web/app.js`, `web/app2.js`, `web/comfort.js`, `web/reports.js`: page registry, router, API calls, HTML templates, forms and event delegation.
- `web/charts.js`, `web/charts2.js`: dependency-free SVG charts and the chart CSS injected at runtime.

The source has two sets of page implementations. This is not accidental from the browser’s perspective: later `registerPage` calls replace the earlier entry in the `PAGES` object. The final page behavior is described below.

### Rendering architecture and cascade

The static shell is deliberately small. The root element starts as:

```html
<html lang="en" data-theme="light" data-palette="paper" data-font="lora">
```

The head runs an inline script before stylesheets load. It reads `localStorage['ledger-theme']`; `system` is resolved immediately through `prefers-color-scheme`, `dark` stays dark, and every other value becomes light. The same script adds `sidebar-collapsed` when `localStorage['ledger-sidebar-collapsed'] === '1'`. This is the first-paint state and prevents a light/dark or expanded/collapsed flash while the API is still loading.

Stylesheets are linked in this exact order:

```text
/fonts/fonts.css
/styles.css
/comfort.css
/receipt-lookup.css
/paper.css
/dark.css
/sidebar.css
/reports.css
```

The order matters because most selectors have equal specificity and the later sheet wins. `styles.css` establishes a dark-oriented token set and generic cards, buttons, tables, forms and modals. `comfort.css` then defines the actual spacious dashboard structure, replaces the root tokens for both dark and light, changes the sidebar from a flex child to a fixed rail, and tightens component geometry. `receipt-lookup.css` adds purchase-lookup pieces without changing the base philosophy. `paper.css` is later than both generic layers and changes the light root into warm paper; it also restyles logo, headings, cards, hero surfaces, rules, avatars and bars. `dark.css` is loaded after paper, but nearly all of its rules begin with `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, so they do not affect the light result. `sidebar.css` is last and therefore controls final desktop rail width, collapsed behavior, readability overrides and collapse control geometry. `reports.css` is last for report components.

A useful mental model for a reconstruction is:

```text
index.html preload state
       │
       ▼
styles.css generic variables + generic component defaults
       │ later equal-specificity rules
       ▼
comfort.css final structure, spacing, light variables, forms, modal layout
       │
       ▼
receipt-lookup.css purchase details additions
       │
       ▼
paper.css light paper tokens + warm editorial overrides
       │ dark selectors inactive in light mode
       ▼
dark.css (no light effect)
       │
       ▼
sidebar.css final rail width/collapse/readability
       │
       ▼
reports.css report geometry
       │
       ▼
charts.js runtime style element (.ax-label, .donut-num, .heat-grid)
```

There are two important override traps. First, `comfort.css` is minified into broad selectors and appears before `paper.css`, so an implementation that copies only the `paper.css` tokens will miss the structural rules from comfort. Second, `comfort.js` is loaded last among scripts and calls `registerPage` for `overview`, `subscriptions`, `accounts`, `settings`, `future` and `typography`, replacing the implementations registered earlier by `app.js` or `app2.js`. A visual rebuild should reproduce the final comfort pages rather than accidentally rendering the earlier page templates.

### Final light tokens

At light startup, `comfort.css` first sets the following general light values on `:root[data-theme=light]`: `--bg #f4f6f8`, `--bg-soft #f7f9fb`, `--panel #fff`, `--panel-2 #edf2f5`, `--text #283e4d`, `--muted #617584`, `--faint #718491`, `--border #d7e1e7`, `--border-soft #e7edf1`, `--accent #557b9b`, `--accent-2 #7596aa`, `--green #4e8070`, `--red #af5654`, `--amber #95733d`, `--cyan #5c889c`, `--shadow 0 12px 45px #2a4f6810`, `--soft-accent #e9f0f4`, `--ink #223f51`, `--rail #bbd0df`, and `color-scheme: light`.

When the default `data-palette="paper"` is active, `paper.css` later replaces the palette with these exact final values:

| Token | Final light paper value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `--bg` | `#fffaf4` | warm page background |
| `--bg-soft` | `#fbf5ed` | secondary background, input surfaces, rail |
| `--panel` | `#fffdf9` | card and modal surface |
| `--panel-2` | `#f7ede3` | secondary card, button and selected surface |
| `--text` | `#373a32` | main body text |
| `--muted` | `#737365` | supporting text and labels |
| `--faint` | `#868274` | least prominent labels |
| `--border` | `#2b3b49` | deliberate dark ink rule |
| `--border-soft` | `#71808b` | quieter rule |
| `--accent` | `#656c48` | olive action and emphasis color |
| `--accent-2` | `#989772` | secondary olive/sand accent |
| `--green` | `#53725e` | positive amount and personal tint |
| `--red` | `#a35642` | danger, negative amount |
| `--amber` | `#9c7f37` | warning and deductible amount |
| `--cyan` | `#526f76` | chart/cool informational accent |
| `--soft-accent` | `#f8ece2` | warm selected/inlay surface |
| `--ink` | `#30372f` | strongest editorial text |
| `--rail` | `#b8b294` | expected-spend rail and subdued chart mark |
| `--shadow` | `0 4px 16px #574b2f07` | very quiet paper shadow |
| `--rule-width` | `.5px` | thin paper rules from comfort |
| `--sidebar-rule-width` | `.75px` | sidebar separator |

The final paper chart palette is `--chart-1 #7e8a63`, `--chart-2 #ae8d58`, `--chart-3 #6d8c88`, `--chart-4 #b78357`, `--chart-5 #a9ab82`, `--chart-6 #8e8773`, `--chart-7 #798170`, `--chart-8 #b2a587`, with `--heat-rgb: 106,127,93`. These values are used by `donutChart` and `heatMap` through CSS variables. Do not replace them with the generic blue/purple colors from `styles.css` when reproducing the paper view.

The paper layer also gives the body a tiny `letter-spacing: .02px`. It uses an almost white warm background rather than a beige block; the warmth comes from low-contrast peach surfaces, olive ink and restrained shadows. Borders are intentionally darker than a typical low-contrast dashboard, like fine printed rules on paper.

### Typography and metrics

The default body stack in the final comfort layer is `'Avenir Next', 'Segoe UI', system-ui, sans-serif`, at `15px` with `1.55` line-height and `letter-spacing: -.12px`. The source does not fetch fonts from a CDN. `fonts.css` serves local WOFF2 files with `font-display: swap`: Lora, Manrope and Nunito Sans each declare weights 400, 500, 600 and 700 from a bundled face file. `Avenir Next` is a system fallback, not a bundled web font.

The `data-font` attribute controls the user’s selection. `data-font=nunito` changes the body to Nunito Sans; `data-font=manrope` changes it to Manrope; `data-font=lora` leaves the body in the comfort sans stack but applies Lora to `.welcome h2`, `.page-intro h2`, `.stat-value`, `.modal h2` and `.logo-name`. The Lora selectors use `font-weight: 500` and `letter-spacing: -.7px`. This is a deliberate distinction: Lora is an editorial display treatment, not the font for every line of UI copy.

Paper then assigns Lora to the logo (`font-size: 30px`, `font-weight: 600`, `letter-spacing: -1.2px`), welcome heading (`31px`, weight 500, `-.7px`) and card headings (`16px`, weight 500). `comfort.css` supplies the baseline logo at `28px`, weight 650, `letter-spacing: -1.5px`, and `paper.css` wins for paper mode. The logo word receives `transform: scaleY(.84)` and `transform-origin: left bottom`; the small dot after “ledger” is colored separately.

Key paper-scale metrics are:

- body: `15px / 1.55` in the comfort layer;
- topbar title: `14px`, weight 600;
- welcome heading: `31px` Lora on paper;
- page intro heading: `26px`, weight 550 before Lora selection;
- stat value: `31px`, weight 550; hero stat values: `34px`; paper changes them to Lora and weight 500;
- card heading: `16px` Lora, normal casing in paper;
- small/support copy: 11–13px, usually `var(--muted)`;
- table body: 13px after comfort; table headers 10px uppercase;
- modal heading: 22px after comfort, weight 550, `letter-spacing: -.5px`;
- authentication heading: 27px, weight 550;
- chart axis labels: 9.5px from runtime chart CSS, with paper/dark token fill;
- utility uppercase labels: roughly 9–11px with 1.1–1.4px tracking.

The font comparison page is itself a design reference. It presents three columns at desktop: Nunito (“Friendly & rounded”), Manrope (“Clear & modern”) and Lora (“Warm & editorial”). Each sample uses a brand lockup, a “Good afternoon” heading, a `$485.20` sample balance, a rail, two recent activity rows and a muted green “Your future” inlay. The Lora option applies Lora to the brand, headings, balance and sample activity heading, while body details stay simple.

### Shell, logo and sidebar

The shell consists of `#sidebar`, `#main`, a topbar, the dynamic `#view`, a mobile add button, modal root and toast root. `comfort.css` makes the sidebar fixed at the left edge: `position: fixed; inset: 0 auto 0 0; z-index: 50; overflow: auto`, with `width: var(--nav-width)`, `padding: 32px 18px 18px`, and a `var(--panel)` background. The main area has `margin-left: var(--nav-width)`, width `calc(100% - var(--nav-width))` and at least viewport height.

The paper logo row is separated from navigation by a thin border. It has `padding-bottom: 23px`, `margin-bottom: 8px`, `gap: 9px`, and a bottom border in `var(--border)`. The 44-square logo mark has no fill in paper mode, a one-rule border, a 3px radius, olive `L` and 28px Georgia-like glyph. The glyph itself is shifted two pixels right by `.ledger-glyph { transform: translateX(2px) }`. The dot is terracotta (`#ad7956`). The word is Lora; the subtitle is 10px italic Georgia and reads “A little more peace of mind.”

Below the logo is an owner row with a 34px avatar and “Your personal space” plus a small status line. In normal mode comfort says “Your private Ledger”; demo mode changes it to “A safe space to explore.” The owner row begins with `padding-top: 19px` in paper mode.

Navigation links use a 20px icon column, 12px gap, 10px vertical padding, 3px vertical margin, and 14px font size. Paper gives links a 5px radius. The active link uses `background: var(--soft-accent)`, strongest ink and a 3px inset copper rule (`#c18f68`), while its icon uses `var(--accent)`. The sidebar groups are “A closer look” and “Your setup,” rendered as 9px uppercase labels with 1.4px tracking. “More insights” is a native `<details>`/`<summary>` containing Personal, Business and Reports; its icon and disclosure arrow need to remain discoverable.

The final desktop width is governed by `sidebar.css`, which is loaded after comfort. Its base `:root { --nav-width: 248px; }` wins over comfort’s earlier 232px declaration. At widths from 701px through 900px, the later sidebar media rule sets `--nav-width: 220px`. On mobile, comfort’s explicit `#sidebar { width: 240px; }` applies while it becomes a drawer. Therefore the effective desktop widths are 248px above 900px and 220px from 701–900px; the sidebar’s earlier comfort declarations of 206px and 185px do not win because the later sidebar variable has equal specificity and later source order.

Desktop collapse is a compact icon rail, not a hidden navigation. `html.sidebar-collapsed` sets `--nav-width: 78px`, and the main margin follows it. The sidebar keeps the logo mark, all nav icons, the More insights affordance, Appearance and Add transaction controls. Labels, owner text, count badges, section headings, footnote and expanded More insights text are hidden. Links center their icons; the More summary centers its icon and hides the arrow. Open child links inside a collapsed More section are hidden until the rail is expanded. The collapse button itself sits absolutely at `top: 84px`, `right: 10px`, with a 28px minimum height, small paper button styling, and the `‹` icon rotated 180 degrees when collapsed. It changes `aria-expanded`, label, title and visible text between “Collapse” and “Expand.”

The inline preload script applies the collapsed class before paint. `comfort.js` later binds the button, persists `ledger-sidebar-collapsed` as `1` or `0`, expands when a collapsed More summary or child link is activated, and deliberately leaves the mobile drawer logic separate. On mobile, the collapse control is hidden. The mobile menu button toggles `body.nav-open`; the sidebar slides from `translateX(-100%)` to zero, and `#nav-shade` becomes a fixed z-index 49 overlay. At max-width 700px, `#main` has no left margin, topbar is 63px high with 19px horizontal padding, and the floating add button is 53px square at right 22px/bottom 25px.

### Main geometry and common surfaces

`#topbar` in comfort is 78px high, static rather than sticky, with 42px horizontal padding, a thin bottom rule and a plain paper background. The breadcrumb says “Your money /”; the current page title is 14px. Right-side controls include sync, export on desktop, Link account on desktop, and the owner avatar. The generic stylesheet’s sticky, blurred topbar is superseded by comfort’s static rule; do not reintroduce blur for the paper target.

The view has maximum width 1420px, `padding: 30px 42px 70px`, and auto horizontal margin. At max-width 1150px it changes to 27px side padding and 25px top padding. At max-width 700px it is `padding: 23px 19px 100px`. Generic grids use 19px gaps in comfort. Two-, three- and four-column grids are available; at max-width 900px the hero grid becomes two columns with the primary card spanning the row, the home section becomes one column, forecast becomes one column, and settings becomes one column. At max-width 700px all common grids become one column.

Cards are paper panels with one half-pixel rule, 7px radius in paper mode, and `box-shadow: var(--shadow)`. Comfort’s card padding is 22px 24px, with 19px padding at max-width 1150px and 19px at mobile. Card headings are sentence case in comfort/paper, use Lora, and align any `.h3-extra` supporting label to the side. The source uses hairline rules for table rows, transactions, bills, footers, disclosures and the welcome divider. Rounded corners exist, but paper mode keeps them modest instead of pill-heavy.

Buttons in comfort are 13px, 9px radius, 9px 14px padding and no shadow. Paper changes radius to 5px. Primary buttons use a dark olive `#626d4b` with warm near-white text `#f8f4e7`; hover darkens to `#505d3f`. Ghost buttons are transparent. Inputs are 14px, at least 41px high in comfort, with paper 5px radius, `var(--bg-soft)` background and a dark thin border. Visible focus uses a 3px accent outline or box shadow from the comfort rules; preserve visible keyboard focus.

The modal is a centered fixed backdrop, originally z-index 90 with dark translucent overlay; comfort sets width `min(540px,96vw)`, 27px padding, 20px radius and max-height controlled by the viewport. The modal root sets `#app.inert` and the mobile add button inert, locks body overflow, returns focus to the trigger on close, closes on Escape or backdrop click, and traps Tab within visible controls. The paper layer changes modal radius to 9px. Toasts are fixed bottom-right, max width 340px; paper gives them a 6px radius.

### Home page: cards, inlays and lines

The final Home page comes from `comfort.js`, not the earlier `app.js` Overview renderer. It fetches overview, monthly plan, subscriptions, recent transactions, six-month cashflow and goals in parallel. It computes the month using the local browser date, greets by time of day (“Good morning,” “Good afternoon,” or “Good evening”), and optionally includes the configured owner name.

The welcome row is a flex row with a 31px Lora heading and a small uppercase month period pill. Paper gives it a bottom rule, `padding-bottom: 23px`, and `margin-bottom: 24px`. The month pill becomes transparent, gets a left border, 10px uppercase type, 19px left padding and muted ink.

The first visual row is `.hero-grid`, three cards with columns `1.3fr 1fr 1fr`, 18px gap and 23px bottom margin. Cards have a minimum height of 169px. Paper gives each a four-pixel top rule and a subtle translucent white gradient from upper left. Their light backgrounds are distinct inlays:

- primary plan card: `rgba(255,247,220,.62)`, top border `#947132`, value `#626642`;
- spent card: `rgba(255,225,208,.50)`, top border `#97532f`, value `#9b6038`;
- net-worth card: `rgba(225,243,232,.50)`, top border `#48634f`, value `#4e6958`.

The primary card says either “Room in your monthly plan,” “Above your monthly plan,” or “Your month, accounted for.” It displays the absolute difference when a monthly target exists, otherwise the current expected total. Its helper line explains tracked/spent/pending amounts. If a target exists, `.spend-rail` is 5px high with olive posted spend and sand expected spend segments; if no target exists, a small “Set a monthly spending plan →” action appears. The footer line says “Tracked commitments only · other spending may still come up.” The spent card uses “Spent so far” and a tiny dot/status line; the net-worth card says “Your net worth” and links to “See what’s possible →.”

If subscription candidates or price reviews exist, a review strip follows the hero row. In the final paper cascade it is `#fff0e8`, with a `#f7dcca` badge and terracotta text such as `#a56c3f`; comfort’s earlier `#fff8e9`/`#f7e7c5` values are superseded. Its left edge remains a fine border rather than a loud alert. A second strip appears when there are no accounts, prompting “Make yourself at home” and Add an account. These strips add context but do not change the core card layout.

The rest of Home uses `.home-section` with columns `minmax(0,1.55fr) minmax(260px,1fr)` and 19px gap. `.home-cards` is `display: contents`, so the four cards are placed by odd/even child selectors into alternating left/right columns. The cards are:

1. **Recent activity.** Each row has a colored merchant avatar, display name, optional original bank name for an applied purchase split, compact category summary, date and pending/transfer label, plus a tabular money value. Applied mixed receipts are summarized as “Split across N budgets,” where N is distinct category IDs. A footer links to all transactions.
2. **Still to come.** Subscription bills use a square day chip, merchant, cadence and expected amount. The footer shows total expected and links to Subscriptions.
3. **Money in, money out.** A six-month hand-rolled SVG bar chart compares posted income with spending. The note explicitly says transfers stay out.
4. **A little closer.** Up to three savings goals show percentage bars, saved/target amounts and a link to goals. Paper resets the fourth card to `var(--panel)` and gives its progress bar `#a38e5f`; the earlier comfort lavender mix is overridden.

Do not make the home page a generic grid of identical white panels. The paper identity comes from the three different hero inlays, hairline dividers, Lora display values, olive/copper/green meaning, and the deliberately quiet fourth-card surface.

### Pages and controls

#### Business and Personal

`app.js` registers Business and Personal and nothing later replaces them. Business fetches business summary and eight-month business cashflow. It presents four stat cards: Revenue TTM, Expenses TTM, Profit TTM and estimated tax set-aside. Below are a revenue-versus-expenses bar chart, deductible-spend detail, top clients/income sources table and expense-breakdown donut. Business values use the business tint border and green/red/amber semantic colors.

Personal fetches personal overview, cashflow, categories, subscriptions and a heatmap. It shows Household net worth, Income this month, Spending this month and Runway, followed by personal cashflow, “Where it goes,” daily spend heatmap and detected subscriptions. The scope pill is managed by `setPill`: in light mode it retains hardcoded purple business (`#6d28d9`) and green personal (`#047857`) text from `styles.css`; the paper palette changes surrounding token-driven surfaces but does not replace those pill colors.

#### Transactions

`app2.js` owns the final Transactions page. It fetches `/transactions` with search, scope, category, since and until filters and also fetches `/receipts`. The filter row has a merchant/note search field, All/Business/Personal scope select, category select, date range fields, Clear action and total count. Enter in search navigates with the current value; other selects and dates navigate immediately. A collapsible “Clarify purchases” summary appears above the table.

The table columns are Date, Name, Account, Category, Scope, Amount and actions. Applied receipt names use `display_name` and show the original charge below; receipt-aware categories can display a split summary. Scope is editable inline with a personal/business select. The Edit action opens a modal. The edit modal includes category, scope, note, recurring checkbox and transfer checkbox. If current receipt allocations exist, it shows each item/category/amount and warns that changing Category applies to the whole charge and replaces the item split. The save payload includes `category_id` only when the category changed from the original; note-only saves therefore preserve allocations. Delete is confirmed. Pagination uses Newer/Older buttons and shows the current slice.

The Add transaction modal is comfort’s override of the earlier app2 modal. It starts with transaction kind (Money out, Money in, Transfer out, Transfer in), amount, name/merchant, date limited to today, account, category and an optional note disclosure. It derives the signed amount from kind, marks transfers from the kind, posts to `/transactions`, remembers the last account in local storage and returns to the current page. If no account exists, the add flow opens the manual-account modal first.

#### Budgets

Budgets remain the app2 implementation. The page explains that monthly envelopes reset each calendar month, offers New budget, and groups cards under Business budgets, Personal budgets and Combined budgets. Each card shows category icon/name, scope tag, spent versus month limit, progress bar, remaining or overage, percentage and delete action. An empty state offers Create your first budget.

The New budget modal requires an expense category, scope (personal, business or all) and positive monthly limit. Save validates a nonzero limit, posts `/budgets`, closes and navigates back to Budgets. Delete is confirmed before `/budgets?id=...` DELETE.

#### Goals

Goals remain the app2 implementation. A goal card shows name, scope, completed trophy where applicable, green progress bar, saved of target, percentage, projected date, monthly plan and either a Contribute action or Complete message. The New savings goal modal accepts name, target, already saved, monthly plan, optional target date and personal/business scope. Save posts `/goals`. Contribute asks for an amount and posts `/goals/contribute`; delete is confirmed. The visual language is the same paper card with a green bar and light metadata, with no heavy dashboard decoration.

#### Subscriptions

The comfort implementation replaces app2’s table. It fetches subscriptions, cancellation jobs and worker status. The intro reads “Keep what earns its place.” with “Your recurring payments, with room to change your mind.” Summary metrics show monthly commitment, a year at that pace and active count. Candidate repeats appear in a review card; they remain outside the plan until confirmed. Price review rows offer Keep my amount or Use new amount. Active subscriptions are roomy cards with avatar, merchant, next due, scope, amount, cadence, normalized monthly cost and Details/Cancel subscription actions. Canceled records are hidden in a native disclosure.

The subscription modal supports merchant, payment amount, cadence (weekly through custom), next payment, scope, account, and a More details disclosure with management URL, billing channel, custom interval, notes and status. The form distinguishes “Already canceled” from active. Cancellation opens a confirmation modal stating that a worker may require sign-in/provider steps and only marks the service canceled after confirmation. Jobs show status, evidence, safe provider links, refresh and a Continue request action when user attention is needed.

#### Your future

The Future page is comfort’s projection tool. It defaults to `/projections/defaults`, posts to `/projections`, and renders either Net worth or Investments through a segmented control. The chart is a hand-built SVG viewBox `0 0 705 270`: five horizontal guides, labels, a filled base/investment area, solid base/investment line and dashed conservative/optimistic lines. The summary shows the selected future value in a 40px stat (35px mobile), real-value note for net worth, and three scenario cells. A disclosure exposes the year-by-year cash, investments, debt and net worth table.

Controls accept years ahead (1–40 range), monthly cash savings, monthly investment, annual return, inflation, and a Balances & debt disclosure containing starting cash, starting investments, starting debt, debt payment and debt APR. “Use current account balances” resets those inputs. The page explicitly calls the result an illustration rather than a prediction and says taxes, fees, market swings and cash interest are not modeled. The form never moves money.

#### Accounts

The comfort Accounts page fetches active accounts, Plaid items, scheduler status, archived accounts and net-worth history. Its intro says “Your money, together.” and offers Manual account. A sync status line and Connect a bank/Sync now actions precede account cards. Manual cards show type, balance, scope and Update balance; linked cards show Make business/Make personal. Archive removes an account from active totals but retains history. Connections show institution, environment, last checked timestamp and optional Reconnect/Remove actions. Archived accounts appear in a disclosure. Estimated balance history contains a net-worth line chart and an explicit estimate limitation; investment projections do not import live prices or holding-level performance.

The manual account modal accepts name, current balance, type (cash/bank, investment, credit card, loan, other asset) and personal/business scope. Credit and loan balances are entered as owed and subtracted from net worth. Linked bank flow uses Plaid Link, asks for a scope first, allows reconnect, and can offer a sandbox quick-add when configured. The external Plaid script is the only intentional third-party runtime load in this app.

#### Settings and typography

The comfort Settings page is a two-column settings grid that collapses to one column. “Look & feel” contains palette (Warm newsprint or Colorful), font comparison link, theme (system/light/dark), density, and four accent swatches (blue, sage, plum, clay). The home dashboard card lets users toggle Recent activity, Upcoming payments, Cash flow and Goals and move them upward. “The everyday details” saves owner name, monthly spending plan and business tax set-aside percentage. The purchase-details assistant appears as a separate section in the final source, followed by cancellation assistant, expandable bank connection settings and data actions.

The bank form is deliberately careful with secrets. It renders blank credential inputs, shows saved/not-saved status, and the server drops blank credential fields so an empty submission retains an existing value; on save the UI clears both fields. It contains environment, registered HTTPS redirect URL and sync interval. Data actions export a transactions CSV, lock Ledger, load sample data, or permanently reset financial data after confirmation. Demo mode disables real bank linking and cancellation actions.

The typography page has the three font samples described above. It is not a separate global product page in the sidebar; it is reached from Settings and returns to Home. Choosing a font saves `font_family` and returns to Home.

### Configuration and persistence semantics

The backend default configuration in `backend/db.py` is the source of truth for a fresh install:

```json
{
  "theme": "light",
  "accent": "blue",
  "density": "comfortable",
  "font_family": "lora",
  "palette": "paper",
  "home_cards": ["recent", "upcoming", "cashflow", "goals"],
  "monthly_spending_target": 0,
  "plaid_env": "sandbox",
  "sync_interval_minutes": 240,
  "tax_rate_business": 0.253,
  "receipt_lookup_enabled": false,
  "receipt_auto_apply": true,
  "receipt_daily_limit": 10
}
```

The desired initial appearance is therefore light + paper + Lora + comfortable density. These are three distinct axes. `theme` selects light/dark/system; `palette` selects paper/colorful; `font_family` selects body/display typography. Do not collapse them into one “look” value. A query string `?look=paper` forces the paper palette in `applyComfort`, while the saved palette otherwise wins.

Theme persistence is duplicated intentionally. The early inline script reads `ledger-theme` for first paint, while the API config stores `theme` in `config.json`. Once `/api/config` returns, `applyComfort` sets `state.theme`, resolves `system` through the media query, sets `data-theme`, `data-accent`, `data-density`, `data-font` and `data-palette`, updates the theme-color meta tag and writes the selected theme back to `ledger-theme`. `applyTheme` is then reassigned by comfort.js to call `applyComfort({theme})`, so later theme changes flow through the full config path. A reconstruction should preserve this early local-storage read and later server reconciliation.

Sidebar collapse is separate from appearance config. It is stored only as `ledger-sidebar-collapsed` and is applied before the API. There is no backend setting for the rail state. Home card order and visibility are stored in the API config as `home_cards`. Accent, palette, font and density changes are posted through `savePreference`; changes are intended to persist across devices because they live in server config.

### Charts and component seams

Charts are pure functions returning HTML strings, with no chart dependency. `fmtMoney` uses US dollars and tabular numeric values, compacting thousands to `k`. `barChart` uses a 640×240 viewBox by default, 46px left padding, 10px right, 12px top and 26px bottom; it draws paired income/spend rounded rectangles and four grid intervals, then a legend. `lineChart` defaults to 640×220, pads the value range by 8%, draws a cyan line with area fill and at most six x labels. `donutChart` uses a 160×160 SVG, radius 60, stroke width 20, eight paper chart colors and a legend.

`heatMap` requests 26 weeks, but the source loop runs from `w=weeks` through `w=0`, so it emits 27 seven-day columns aligned to Saturday while labeling the result “26 weeks.” It uses square-root intensity from `--heat-rgb`, makes future cells transparent, and includes a less-to-more legend. `projectionChart` is local to comfort and uses the paper tokens through CSS variables. Runtime chart CSS is appended as a style element after all linked stylesheets, so its `.ax-label` font size/fill and `.heat-grid` layout should remain available.

Recommended component boundaries for a rebuild are:

```text
AppShell
├── ThemeBootstrap       localStorage first paint + API reconciliation
├── Sidebar              nav, More disclosure, collapse rail, mobile drawer
├── Topbar               page title, sync/export/link actions
├── Router               PAGES registry, hash navigation, stale-render token
├── Page views           home, business, personal, transactions, budgets,
│                       goals, subscriptions, future, accounts, settings,
│                       typography, reports
├── Surface primitives   Card, Stat, Button, Input, Table, Disclosure, Modal
├── Data visualizations  BarChart, LineChart, DonutChart, HeatMap, Projection
└── API client           JSON request headers, error normalization, auth cookie
```

The router increments `state.renderToken` before each async render. A slower request that finishes after a newer navigation is ignored. It writes `#view` loading and error states and resets the mobile drawer. Keep this concurrency guard; it prevents old page HTML from replacing the current route.

### Responsive behavior matrix

| Width | Sidebar/main | Home and grids | Forms/modal |
|---|---|---|---|
| > 1550px | 248px rail; view top padding becomes 42px | hero cards grow to 187px | normal two-column settings |
| 1151–1550px | 248px rail | 1420px max view, 42px sides | standard controls |
| 901–1150px | 248px rail because final sidebar variable wins | view 27px sides; generic 3/4 grids reduce | forecast side column 250px |
| 701–900px | 220px rail | two-column hero, primary spans both; home one column; forecast/settings one column | subscription actions wrap |
| ≤700px | 240px off-canvas drawer; main full width | all grids one column; hero primary 160px; cards 19px padding | 90dvh modal, 12px backdrop padding, floating add button |

Reduced motion is respected globally in comfort: animations and transitions are disabled and scroll behavior becomes automatic under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`. Dark CSS repeats its own reduced-motion rule but is inactive in the light target.

### Pitfalls and fidelity checklist

1. Preserve stylesheet order. Loading paper before comfort produces the wrong geometry; loading sidebar before comfort loses the final rail width and collapse rules.
2. Preserve the final comfort page registrations. `app.js`’s earlier overview is not the visible Home page once comfort.js loads. The final source has comfort versions of Home, Subscriptions, Accounts and Settings.
3. Do not trust the comments in `styles.css` to describe the final appearance. The comment says “dark-first,” but the default is changed by comfort light and then paper tokens.
4. Treat inline styles in templates as part of the contract. Several grid spans, colors, margins and widths are inline; external CSS must not accidentally override them with broad selectors.
5. Keep `--border` dark enough for paper rules. The design uses half-pixel separators with a dark blue-green ink rather than barely visible gray lines.
6. Keep Lora restrained. It belongs to display headings, logo and selected large values; body and utility text remain sans/Georgia fallbacks.
7. Keep hero surfaces meaningfully distinct: pale yellow/olive plan, peach spent, pale green net worth. Do not flatten them into one panel color.
8. Keep financial semantics readable: green positive values, red negative/danger, amber tax/deductible/warning, copper/terracotta receipt review, cyan chart information, and muted olive paper action.
9. Keep the mobile drawer separate from desktop collapse. `sidebar-collapsed` is ignored by the mobile control; mobile uses `nav-open`, visibility and transform.
10. Keep all navigation discoverable when collapsed. The compact rail hides words but retains icons, accessible labels and title/data-tooltip affordances; More insights expands the rail before revealing its child links.
11. Keep modal focus and inert behavior. The app is designed for keyboard use, including skip link, visible focus rings, Escape close, backdrop close and Tab trapping.
12. Keep the “estimate” language for balance history and “illustration, not a prediction” language for projections. Do not turn computed scenarios into guarantees.
13. Keep demo boundaries visible. The demo banner says “Sample data · Explore freely. Bank linking and agents are off in this preview.”
14. Keep receipt and original transaction identity separate. An applied display name may replace the prominent label, but the original charge remains available in details and category allocations must not duplicate the underlying bank charge.
15. Keep source data out of any reconstruction package. The interface can be reproduced from this source snapshot and synthetic fixtures; no database or config values are needed.

The target is a quiet, warm, editorial finance workspace: fixed paper rail, dark blue-green ink, Lora headings, olive action color, copper review accents, thin printed rules, distinct inlay cards and enough space to read the numbers. The design feels personal because typography and small copy carry the tone, while the layout stays disciplined and functional.

## 7. Backend reconstruction: schemas, accounting, APIs, and agents

### Scope, source pin, and reading rules

This guide reconstructs the Ledger application from the repository snapshot included in this guide. It is intended for an engineer who must remake the backend independently and needs the behavior, invariants, and ordering of implementation. The guide describes what the pinned source actually implements. Statements marked **Aspirational or operationally conditional** describe behavior that depends on a provider, a local worker, deployment configuration, or a future integration and must not be mistaken for a guaranteed behavior in a unit-test-only remake.

The application is a private, single-owner finance dashboard. The backend is standard-library Python with SQLite and an HTTP server; the web UI is vanilla JavaScript. There is no required framework, ORM, queue service, cloud database, or external API in the test environment. The normal development entry point is `python3 backend/server.py`. The database and JSON configuration live below `backend/data` unless `LEDGER_DATA_DIR` selects another directory. A demo run uses a separate temporary data directory and `LEDGER_DEMO=1`; this is important because demo mode must never exercise real bank, receipt, or cancellation actions.

The included snapshot includes the receipt and cancellation subsystems, Plaid integration, reports, subscriptions, forecasts, auth, scheduler, and the web configuration refinements. It may have later uncommitted files in a working tree, but those are outside this reconstruction. Rebuild against the interfaces and behavior below first, then consult the source files named in each section for exact serialization details.

### Architecture and reconstruction order

The safest reconstruction order is:

1. Build `backend/db.py` and make `init_db()` idempotent. Establish data-directory permissions, SQLite connection settings, base tables, seed categories, and additive migrations.
2. Build `backend/auth.py`, then the request guards in `backend/server.py`. Do this before exposing financial routes.
3. Build transaction and account mutation paths in `server.py`, including account balance updates and manual override columns.
4. Build analytics and reports. These are read models over transactions, accounts, categories, and (when valid) receipt allocations.
5. Build subscriptions. Its scan and monthly-plan logic depends on the transaction semantics and categories.
6. Build forecasts. It consumes account balances and uses explicit user inputs rather than silently replacing them with analytics.
7. Build `plaid_client.py` behind strict environment and credential guards. Make ingestion and refresh transactional and idempotent before attempting any live connection.
8. Build receipts and cancellations as persistent, evidence-first workflows. Their tables must exist even when workers are disabled.
9. Build scheduler and optional local workers. Keep provider calls outside tests and outside demo mode.
10. Add route serialization and UI integration only after the domain modules have deterministic tests.

The modules intentionally use small functions and SQLite transactions instead of a service framework. `db._conn()`, `q()`, `q1()`, and `ex()` are the low-level conventions. New modules expose an idempotent `init_schema()` so application startup and tests can safely call initialization more than once. Use `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` for operations that reserve a resource or reconcile financial state; a plain lookup followed by a later write is not sufficient under concurrent sync or worker requests.

### Configuration, storage, and database schema

`backend/db.py` computes `DATA_DIR` from `LEDGER_DATA_DIR` or the repository's `backend/data`, then derives `DB_PATH` and `CONFIG_PATH`. `_conn()` creates the directory with restrictive permissions, opens SQLite with a 30-second timeout, sets `row_factory=sqlite3.Row`, enables foreign keys, enables WAL, and attempts to make the database file mode 0600. This is a local privacy boundary, not an encryption layer.

The default JSON configuration includes empty Plaid client ID and secret fields, `plaid_env` defaulting to `sandbox`, display preferences, USD currency, an empty Plaid redirect URI, a four-hour sync interval, owner name, month-start day, business tax rate, spending target, and receipt controls. Receipt controls are `receipt_lookup_enabled=False`, `receipt_auto_apply=True`, and `receipt_daily_limit=10`. `save_config()` accepts only keys in `DEFAULT_CONFIG`, writes a temporary file, flushes and fsyncs it, and replaces the old config. Empty credential patch values are dropped, so clearing a form field retains an already saved credential. This behavior is deliberate and prevents a masked or blank UI value from overwriting a secret.

`public_config()` reads the private configuration and returns independent `plaid_client_id_saved` and `plaid_secret_saved` booleans, plus `plaid_configured` when both exist. It removes the secret and always returns an empty client-ID value. The booleans mean **Saved**, not Validated: they only indicate stored nonempty values. Production versus sandbox remains separately exposed as `plaid_env`. A frontend should use a fresh `/api/config` response when deciding whether to start bank linking; a stale captured configuration can incorrectly redirect to settings even after another tab saved credentials.

The base schema is:

- `items`: local institution connection rows, with Plaid item ID, institution name, environment, access token, cursor, and timestamps. Access tokens are private storage and are never serialized to the client.
- `accounts`: an item-owned account with local ID, display and official names, account type/subtype, `scope` constrained to `personal` or `business`, mask, balance, ISO currency, Plaid account ID, and `archived`. Foreign-key deletion follows the item.
- `categories`: seeded expense and income categories with name, kind, icon, and tax-deductibility flag. `Personal Care` is a seeded personal expense category; business categories include Software & SaaS and the other business operating categories.
- `transactions`: account-owned financial facts. The stored sign convention is that a negative amount is an outflow and a positive amount is income or a credit. Columns include local account, scope, amount, posted date, name, merchant, category, pending, recurring, note, optional split scope/amount, Plaid transaction ID, and creation time. Additive columns include `is_transfer`, `pending_transaction_id`, `is_transfer_override`, `scope_override`, `category_override`, and `name_override`.
- `budgets`: category budget, scope (`personal`, `business`, or `all`), monthly limit, and period.
- `goals`: target and saved amounts, monthly plan, target date, scope, optional account, completion timestamp, and creation time.

Indexes cover posted dates and scopes. Plaid transaction IDs are unique. Migrations add columns if missing rather than dropping or rewriting real rows. `reset_all()` deletes financial and workflow rows while keeping configuration and categories. The server exposes `/api/data/reset` behind the authenticated HTTP guard and refuses active cancellation jobs or linked bank items, but `reset_all()` itself has no demo check; a remake should treat this as an explicitly destructive authenticated route rather than assume it is demo-only.

Manual transaction edits are represented as overrides instead of being overwritten by future Plaid refreshes. `scope_override` and `is_transfer_override` are nullable: `NULL` means the latest Plaid classification is authoritative, while a non-null value means preserve the user's choice. `category_override` and `name_override` serve the same purpose for categorization and presentation. A manual category can be explicitly uncategorized only when the application records a lock/override state; otherwise a null category is indistinguishable from “no provider category yet.” Account moves update transactions lacking a scope override and invalidate receipt evidence for affected transactions.

### Money, signs, transfers, scopes, and dates

Ledger stores many base amounts as SQLite `REAL`, but domain boundaries validate finite values and cap their magnitude. New reports convert to integer cents through `Decimal` with half-up quantization before aggregation. Preserve the current REAL storage and report-side cents conversion for an exact reconstruction; an all-integer storage refactor is optional future work and would need compatibility migration.

A transaction amount `< 0` is spending. Analytics turns it into positive spend by negating it. A transaction amount `> 0` is income, a refund, or an account credit and does not reduce gross spending in Reports. Pending transactions are excluded from historical spend, net worth reconstruction, and category analysis. Transfers are excluded from analytics and reports, even if their amount is negative. Posted dates after the local current date are excluded from historical calculations; this applies to future-dated posted rows as well as pending rows. The subscription monthly plan can show pending commitments separately, but it still excludes future posted history from paid spending.

Every account and transaction has a scope. Most account-derived transactions inherit the account's scope at insertion. A user can explicitly override transaction scope; analytics and reports must use the transaction's effective scope, not blindly re-read the account. Scope filters are optional and mean all scopes when omitted. Archived accounts remain part of historical reports and all-time reports, but are excluded from active balance views and receipt lookup eligibility. Plaid refresh is item-scoped and still processes an item even when one of its accounts is archived; archiving affects the account's active presentation and eligibility, not the item's refresh loop.

Transactions cannot be inserted with a posted date after today through the normal server mutation route. Existing imported rows can still be future-dated, so read paths explicitly guard against them. The reports module accepts an internal `as_of` seam for deterministic tests; HTTP uses today's local date. Month boundaries are calendar boundaries, including leap February and December-to-January rollover. Do not use a fixed “last ten years” cutoff for all-time reporting.

### HTTP server, auth, and security boundary

`backend/server.py` serves the SPA and JSON APIs with Python's threaded HTTP server. It binds to loopback by default. Binding `0.0.0.0` is permitted only in the intended container environment, detected through `/.dockerenv`. `LEDGER_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` can define the accepted external origin. Responses set `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, and a restrictive Permissions Policy. The content-security policy allows the local application plus the Plaid CDN where required.

The JSON body reader caps request bodies at 1 MiB, rejects invalid JSON and non-object JSON payloads, and rejects non-finite JSON constants. Mutating requests must carry `X-Ledger-Request: 1`, and the Origin must be loopback or the configured exact public origin. Setup is limited to localhost. Protected API routes require a valid owner session except in explicit demo mode. Health and auth status are intentionally public; credentials, access tokens, and raw secrets are never returned.

`auth.py` creates a one-owner record and sessions. Passwords use scrypt where available, with PBKDF2 fallback. Session tokens are random and stored hashed with SHA-256; cookies are HttpOnly, SameSite, and scoped appropriately. Login failures are rate-limited with a five-failure/lockout-window policy. Sessions expire after the configured lifetime, are refreshed on validation, can be revoked by logout, and are cleaned up. Login errors are generic to avoid account enumeration. The first setup is one-shot and requires a password of at least twelve characters.

The route surface includes health/auth/config, accounts/items/categories, transactions and CSV, summaries, budgets/goals, monthly plan, reports, projections, subscriptions, cancellations, receipts, and sync. The HTTP route layer applies the same guards whether a request came from the UI or another HTTP client; domain helpers generally assume their caller has performed those checks, so direct module calls are not universally demo-guarded. Plaid link-token, exchange, and sandbox-token routes have explicit demo guards; the item-refresh route relies on the authenticated HTTP boundary and the helper's environment/credential checks rather than a universal demo guard. Never expose an access token in a response.

### Accounts and transaction mutation behavior

Manual accounts validate name, type, scope, and finite balance. Credit and loan account balances use a liability sign convention: their current balance is stored negative when owed. This makes the account sum suitable for net worth. Positive balances on credit or loan accounts can be assets (for example, an overpayment) and must remain positive; do not classify by account name. The forecast default builder uses account type/subtype, not names such as “First Credit Union checking,” to distinguish cash, investment, and debt.

Manual transaction insertion requires an active account, a finite nonzero amount within the configured magnitude limit, a valid posted date not later than today, bounded text fields, and a valid category when supplied. It derives scope from the account unless the caller provides a valid explicit scope. Insertion updates the manual account balance and records explicit transfer/category overrides where appropriate. A safe subscription scan may run after a successful insertion; scan failures are isolated from the transaction commit.

Updates flow through `receipt_store.manual_update()` so receipt evidence can be invalidated consistently. Allowed fields include category, name, note, scope, recurring, and transfer status. JSON booleans are accepted for boolean fields and normalized rather than rejected as ordinary integers. A manual category edit deactivates accepted receipt allocations and records the explicit category override. Scope or transfer edits invalidate receipt jobs because the financial fingerprint changed. Plaid later uses `COALESCE(override, provider_value)` for these fields.

Deleting an account/item is guarded when cancellation jobs or linked workflows make removal unsafe. Deleting a transaction also removes or invalidates receipt allocations and updates manual balance state. `remove_item()` detaches goals and subscriptions before cascading item-owned accounts and transactions. A detached subscription receives a normalized merchant/scope key without the deleted account component; learning mappings are retained only when doing so cannot produce an unsafe collision.

### Analytics and the Reports contract

`backend/analytics.py` is the dashboard read model. `_flows()` sums positive income and negative-to-positive spend, filtering out pending, transfers, and future posted dates, with an optional scope. `overview()` reports current and previous month flows, active-account net worth, savings rate, and a non-business runway. Active balances include negative liabilities; archived accounts are omitted from the current net-worth snapshot.

`net_worth_series()` begins with active balances and reconstructs prior month values using posted, non-pending, non-transfer flows. Future posted history is excluded. It is an approximation based on available transaction history and account balances; it does not pretend to be a full statement-reconciliation engine. Cashflow series, category breakdown, budgets, heatmaps, and monthly matrices use the same filters. Expense category totals consume valid receipt allocations when available; otherwise they fall back to the parent transaction category. Receipt allocations partition a charge once, so a mixed Amazon order can be split across categories without duplicating its total.

`backend/reports.py` implements `spending_report(year=None, scope=None, as_of=None)`. Scope must be omitted, `personal`, or `business`. A year is a strict integer or digit-only string from 1900 through the current year; the HTTP layer rejects malformed strings such as a float representation. The default is the current calendar year. The query reads all stored transactions without joining only active accounts, so archived history is included. Eligible rows have negative amounts, `pending=0`, `is_transfer=0`, and `posted <= as_of`. Positive income/refunds never offset gross spending.

The response is:

```text
{
  year, as_of, scope,
  available_years: descending eligible selector years plus current/requested,
  year_total, all_time_total,
  first_recorded_date, last_recorded_date, transaction_count,
  months: 12 entries {month, spend, transaction_count, is_future},
  categories: [{id, name, months: 12 monetary entries, total}]
}
```

All money is serialized as two-decimal values. `year_total` equals the sum of month spend and the sum of category totals. `all_time_total` includes every eligible stored date, including dates older than ten years and even dates before 1900 if such rows exist; those ancient years are deliberately excluded from `available_years` because the selector only accepts 1900 onward. Empty years return zero totals, twelve zero months, empty categories, null first/last dates, and count zero. Future months in the selected year are explicit zero entries with `is_future=true`; a future-dated row within the current month is also excluded and leaves that month's spend unchanged. This contract supports Dec 31/Jan 1 separation and leap-day February without special UI logic.

### Subscription detection and lifecycle

`backend/subscriptions.py` has a richer recurring-commitment model than the older `analytics.detect_recurring()` helper. The latter is a lightweight dashboard signal. The subscription scanner must be conservative because an early candidate is useful, while an automatically activated grocery or fuel pattern creates a false fixed expense.

Subscription rows store merchant, scope, optional account, amount, cadence, optional custom interval, billing day, next due date, status, confidence, reason, management URL, billing channel, notes, observed amount, price-review state, ignored price, normalized identity key, and observation timestamps. Statuses are `candidate`, `active`, `cancel_requested`, `canceled`, and `dismissed`. Review decisions include confirm/activate, dismiss, cancellation transitions, `accept_price`, and `keep_price`. A review/learning table suppresses repeatedly dismissed detections without deleting the underlying transactions.

Merchant normalization lowercases, strips punctuation/noise, and builds an exact identity from normalized merchant plus scope plus account when known. Matching is exact normalized identity with amount tolerance, not arbitrary substring matching. Amount tolerance is the larger of fifty cents and twenty percent. A manual subscription without an account can be reused when there is exactly one matching manual record in the same scope and amount range; if multiple manual records make identity ambiguous, scanning does not select one and does not create an unsafe duplicate.

The scanner considers negative, posted, non-pending, non-transfer transactions and skips future dates. It groups by exact normalized merchant/scope/account. It requires at least three distinct calendar-cycle regular posted charges for autoactivation, a supported regular cadence, strong interval fit, amount spread no greater than about ten percent, confidence at least .82, and a recent observation within roughly 2.5 cadence intervals (with a minimum window of sixty days). Known merchants can produce a single-charge **candidate**, but the high-sensitivity shortcut never autoactivates from one charge. Custom cadence is always a candidate unless explicitly confirmed by the user. Grocery, supermarket, gas/fuel, dining, restaurant, and coffee categories or merchant signals are excluded from automatic activation. Existing detections are downgraded to candidate when they fail these new criteria, unless explicit user confirmation is recorded.

Cadence inference recognizes weekly, biweekly, monthly, quarterly, annual, and custom intervals. Cadence matching allows roughly twenty-two percent or three days of interval error. Custom intervals must be one through 366 days; two charges years apart that infer an unsupported interval are skipped gracefully, so one bad group cannot abort a whole scan. Monthly due dates preserve a January 31-style anchor by clamping only the target month's day to its final day and restoring the anchor in later months. User-corrected cadence and due date remain authoritative.

The scan's confidence combines observation count, interval fit, and amount variation. The inferred amount uses the latest chronological observed charge. For a manual subscription, active amount, cadence, due date, and anchor remain unchanged; a latest charge that differs creates a price review with `observed_amount` and `price_review=true`. For detected active subscriptions, the known commitment remains in totals while the latest differing observation creates the same review. `accept_price` changes the active amount and clears the review. `keep_price` preserves the active amount and stores the ignored observation so the same charge does not reprompt. Historical old amounts are not reconsidered after acceptance; only the latest chronological observation is evidence. A normal confirm/dismiss path remains unchanged.

`listing(scope)` separates active and cancellation-requested commitments, candidates, canceled subscriptions, monthly totals, personal/business totals, and `price_reviews`. `monthly_plan(scope, month)` queries expense transactions in the month, excluding future posted history. It reports paid spend, pending spend separately, and upcoming expected subscription dues. Due matching uses exact normalized merchant/scope identity, optional account, amount tolerance, and a due-date tolerance of the larger of three days and twenty percent of the cadence. A `used_tx_ids` set ensures one transaction reconciles against at most one due event/subscription. Paid and upcoming entries sort by due date. `total_expected` is paid spend plus pending spend plus upcoming commitments, and `monthly_cost` is the compatibility alias for the subscription commitment total.

### Forecast math

`backend/forecasts.py` intentionally models user-entered cash savings, investments, and debt contributions independently. It does not infer monthly contributions from current spend or silently use the account balance as a contribution. `defaults(scope)` validates scope and uses active accounts. Account type/subtype determines investment accounts: investment, brokerage, 401k, 403b, IRA, Roth, and securities-like types are investment balances. Positive balances from ordinary checking/savings and even positive credit/loan balances count as cash assets. Negative balances count as liabilities. The default identity is therefore `starting_cash + starting_investments - starting_debt` equal to the sum of active account balances under the classification.

`project()` validates finite numeric inputs with an absolute magnitude cap, years as an integer from one through 100, nonnegative starting balances/contributions, annual return greater than -100 and at most 100, inflation/debt rates bounded to 100, and other rate inputs finite. Three scenarios use annual return minus three, base, and plus three percentage points. The base annual return can be negative; at -99%, the monthly growth factor remains positive and all scenario outputs remain real and finite. Monthly compounding uses a growth factor derived from `(1 + annual_return/100) ** (1/12)`. Debt interest uses nominal APR divided by twelve, so a 7% APR accrues 7%/12 per month, not an effective annual-to-monthly conversion.

Each scenario independently grows cash savings, investments, and debt. Contributions are added to the corresponding bucket; debt payments reduce debt after interest and are capped so debt cannot become a negative liability from overpayment. Year rows expose contributions, investment value, cash value, debt value, and net value. Real value is nominal net value divided by an inflation factor. Summary and rows are checked for finite values before serialization. These are illustrations, not predictions: the module has no market feed, tax model, volatility model, or repayment schedule beyond the input assumptions.

### Plaid integration and synchronization

`backend/plaid_client.py` maps `sandbox` and `production` to official Plaid endpoints and uses a serialized `_sync_lock` around the whole `refresh_item()` operation. The thirty-second network timeout belongs to `_post()`, which reads private configuration, validates environment and both credentials, sends the provider request, and maps provider failures to safe application errors. Redirect URI errors include actionable guidance without exposing secrets. `_post()` itself does not inspect demo or test environment flags; scheduler and explicit link/sandbox routes guard their paths, but the helper and item-refresh route are not universally demo-guarded, so direct callers must supply their own guard.

Link-token creation requests the transactions product and a long history window, optionally reusing an access token for reconnect and passing the configured HTTPS redirect URI. Public-token exchange obtains the provider item and access token, then fetches accounts. Sandbox token creation is allowed only when the configured environment is sandbox. Account balance mapping makes credit and loan balances negative while preserving positive credit balances as assets.

`ingest_item()` validates scope and environment, exchanges credentials, and starts `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` before lookup/upsert. It can accept an optional existing local item ID. If that ID belongs to a different provider item, the function fails rather than orphaning or mixing data. Otherwise it reuses the existing local item by local ID or Plaid item ID, preserving local item/account IDs, scopes, archive flags, and manual transaction overrides. Accounts upsert provider metadata and authoritative balances, and new accounts are created only when absent. Repeated exchange is idempotent by Plaid IDs.

`sync_transactions()` paginates incremental changes up to its page bound and retries mutation conflicts a limited number of times. `refresh_item()` takes the serialized lock, obtains sync data and account metadata, maps account IDs, and applies removed/added/modified transactions transactionally. Pending transactions can be replaced by a posted transaction using the pending transaction ID. Modified rows preserve `scope_override`, `is_transfer_override`, `category_override`, and `name_override` with `COALESCE`; provider changes update only fields without local overrides. Provider amounts are converted to Ledger's sign convention by negating Plaid's positive debit amount. Every changed financial fingerprint invalidates receipt evidence. Account balances and cursors commit with the transaction.

`remove_item()` refuses removal when cancellation jobs make it unsafe, calls provider removal only when a token exists, detaches goals, detaches subscriptions and rebuilds their normalized key without the deleted account, then cascades the item-owned accounts and transactions. It does not destructively merge duplicate user records. Learning mappings remain only when identity is unambiguous.

### Receipts and exact allocation accounting

Receipt workflows are persistent and local. `receipt_store.py` creates `receipt_jobs`, `receipt_attempts`, and `receipt_allocations`. Job statuses are `queued`, `running`, `needs_user`, `review`, `applied`, `dismissed`, and `failed`. An allocation is an overlay for one parent bank transaction; it is not a child transaction. The parent still contributes to overall totals exactly once. Category reports, budgets, transaction filters, and CSV can use active valid allocations to partition the parent amount.

`financial_fingerprint()` hashes the account, effective scope, signed amount, posted date, pending flag, and transfer flag. `allocation_map(ids)` fails closed unless the allocation belongs to an applied, active job whose stored fingerprint and total still equal the current eligible parent transaction. It rejects pending, transfer, future, income, archived, demo/sandbox, and explicit manual category override conditions where the split would violate user intent. It batches IDs in chunks to avoid SQLite placeholder limits. `decorate_transactions()` exposes applied-only display name and allocation data; queued, running, dismissed, review, failed, and needs-user jobs still expose their statuses and job IDs, but their untrusted proposals cannot change the visible name or category. The ordinary presentation fallback remains explicit name override first, then merchant/name, preserving existing UI labels.

Providers are `amazon`, `apple`, and `google`, detected from the transaction merchant/name. `scan()` only queues when `receipt_lookup_enabled` is true and remains bounded by the configured daily limit. `request()` and `claim_next()` independently enforce the same eligibility: no pending/transfer/future/income transaction, no archived account, no demo or sandbox item, and a valid provider. A job request cannot be used to launch an external lookup for an ineligible transaction.

Daily accounting counts attempts made today, including failures and resumes. An attempt ledger timestamp is required; lifetime attempt counters are insufficient. Stale running jobs recover after the local-time stale window. Claims begin with a write lock, reread the transaction, and return a safe context containing local transaction ID, account scope, currency, and mask, plus a fingerprint and claimed attempt number. The worker must pass `expected_attempt` to `finish()`. A stale worker finishing after a newer claim is rejected and cannot apply or overwrite the new result. Public booleans such as `verified` and `can_apply` are normalized to actual booleans.

A payload is strictly validated before any job state transition: top-level and nested values must be dictionaries, status must be matched/needs_user/failed, item count is at most 100, item descriptions are bounded to 300 characters, item amounts are strict positive integers (no bools, floats, or numeric strings), and their exact cents sum must equal the parent charge. Categories must be expense categories; unknown/null categories cannot autoapply. Confidence is a finite number in [0,1], not a boolean. The message is clamped/validated to 2,000 characters. Receipt evidence fields include HTTPS URL, order ID, purchased-on date, currency, total cents, and card last four where available. A malformed payload must become a failed/review result rather than leaving a claimed job running due to an exception.

Automatic application requires trusted worker verification and a high-confidence identity: matching HTTPS evidence URL/order/date, exact total, currency equal to the transaction currency, account mask present and exactly matching the receipt card last four, match confidence at least .95, every item confidence at least .90, no ambiguity, and automatic application enabled. Missing masks or missing Apple card details can produce a review candidate but cannot autoapply. A known card mismatch never autoapplies. Provider order IDs are unique across transactions; a dismissed prior order releases the reservation for the same transaction while preserving duplicate protection against another transaction.

`review(job_id, decision, category_ids=None)` supports accept or dismiss. For an itemized accept, the optional ordered category list must have exactly the same length as the immutable proposal items and each category must be a valid expense category. The user may correct uncertain categories individually; descriptions, receipt evidence, and cents remain immutable. Manual acceptance may override low confidence or missing-card evidence only when the capture is verified and the transaction identity is not contradicted. A known mismatch cannot be overridden merely by clicking accept. Explicit acceptance can replace a parent manual category; undo restores the prior manual value or fallback state. `undo(transaction_id)` deactivates the applied allocation and restores parent presentation/category state without deleting the bank transaction.

`manual_update()` preserves current scope/transfer/name/category overrides, validates bounded text and booleans, and invalidates receipt allocations on financial edits. A Plaid refresh therefore cannot silently resurrect an old split. The local worker (`receipt_worker.py`) uses a read-only browser bridge, safe provider host allowlists, persistent per-provider profile locks, and no credentials/MFA/mutations.
